title: FERC General Correspondence — Docket P-13526-000: Letter to The Bowersock Mills & Power Company discussing the 08/27/2026 Temporary Water Retention Structure to address failure of Rubber Dam Section No. 2 for the Expanded Kansas River Hydropower Project under P-13526.

FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION
Office of Energy Projects
Division of Dam Safety and Inspections
Chicago Regional Office
In reply refer to: P-13526
September 1, 2026
VIA ELECTRONIC MAIL
Ms. Sarah Hill-Nelson
The Bowersock Mills & Power Company
shn@bowersockpower.com
Re: Expanded Kansas River Hydropower Project (Bowersock) (FERC No. 13526)
- August 27, 2026 - Temporary Water Retention Structure to Address Failure of
Rubber Dam Section #2
Dear Ms. Hill-Nelson:
Your letter dated August 27, 2026, submitted a design package for installation of
AquaFence System at the Expanded Kansas River Hydropower Project (Bowersock),
FERC No. 13526. The purpose of the proposed AquaFence is to provide a temporary
measure for restoring the millpond to normal operating level (Elevation 813.0 feet
NGVD29, approximately 5.5feet) after the rupture of Rubber Dam #2 on July 10th.
Additionally, AquaFence will establish a dry work zone to facilitate the replacement of
the damaged rubber dam with Obermeyer Gates.
The design package included AquaFence System Shop Drawing Review and
Anchorage Design, prepared and certified by your consultant, Lauren A. Kitchen, P.E. of
Olsson; and drawing and specifications for the AquaFence installation along with
structural calculation prepared by AquaFence Inc.
Your consultant confirmed that the structural calculations provided by AquaFence
for the V2400 (7.87-foot) floodwall were reviewed and found the design to be reasonable
as a temporary cofferdam to withstand the anticipated water levels and loads for the
project. The anchors connecting the AquaFence to the existing concrete structure were
designed by your consultant based on the reactions provided in the AquaFence structural
calculations. The reaction loads for the main ground and the side connector anchors, were
provided in the AquaFence calculations. Anchor capacities were determined by using
technical data published by Hilti for the specified anchor system and showed to exceed
the minimum Factor of Safety of 1.5 used in AquaFence design.
Our review of the design report, the drawings and the specifications did not
identify any potential dam safety concerns, and we concur with the proposed work.

2
You are authorized to proceed with the installation of the AquaFence System
assuming you have all necessary permits. Any changes to the plans and specifications
should be coordinated between the Design Engineer and FERC. Any change in the
operation of the project should be properly coordinated with FERC and understood by all
your operators. No changes to the operation of the project can be made to the project until
it is authorized by FERC. Any aberrant conditions encountered during the construction
should be reported to FERC as soon as practical after the situation is discovered, without
interfering with any necessary emergency response.
Regarding the Part 12.10(a)(2) report requested with our July 24, 2026 letter, the
revised due date for submitting it is September 30, 2026. The report should cover the
period from the rubber dam failure through AquaFence installation. The following link
has the outline of the Part 12.10(a)(2) report: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-18/part-
12/section-12.10#p-12.10(a)(2).
File your submittal using the Commission’s eFiling system at
https://www.ferc.gov/ferc-online/overview. When eFiling, select Hydro: Dam Safety and
Chicago Regional Office from the eFiling menu. The cover page of the filing must
indicate that the material was eFiled. For assistance with eFiling, contact FERC Online
Support at FERCOnlineSupport@ferc.gov, (866) 208-3676 (toll free), or (202) 502-8659
(TTY).
You may contact Mr. Paul Kokoszka at (312) 596-4457 (paul.kokoszka@ferc.gov)
or me at (312) 596-4456 if you have questions.
Sincerely,
Marilyn Sabido, P.E.
Regional Engineer

This letter acknowledges multiple filings regarding vegetation management and
aquatic nuisance vegetation management, including your April 3, 2026 and June 3, 2026
filings in response to the Commission’s February 3, 2026 letter (Commission letter)
notifying you of violations of license Article 405 for the Tulloch Hydroelectric Project
No. 2067.1
Additionally, this letter discusses comments and allegations concerning your
implementation of the approved Vegetation Management Plan (VMP)2 and the approved
Aquatic Nuisance Vegetation Management Plan (ANVMP).3 As discussed in more detail

Background
By letter dated February 3, 2026, Commission staff found that implementation of
the approved ANVMP has not achieved the ANVMP goals and objectives and does not
fulfill the requirements of Article 405. Additionally, the approved ANVMP does not
include (1) provisions for training project staff; (2) provisions for advising resource
agencies of aquatic nuisance vegetation populations on lands these agencies manage
within the project boundary and coordinating with these agencies regarding eradication or
control efforts; and (3) provisions for the identification, mapping, management, and
monitoring of wetlands and important habitat, pursuant to Article 405. Commission staff
required you to make the changes necessary to satisfy the requirements of Article 405
with the ANVMP and review the ANVMP in consultation with the required resource
agencies, allowing sufficient time for stakeholder consultation. You are then required to
file any proposed amendments with the Commission for review and approval.
Commission staff also found that you are in violation of Article 405 of the project
license on the basis that: (1) you have failed to file VMP reports as specified by the
Order Modifying and Approving Vegetation Management Plan Pursuant to Article 405
(2008 Order); (2) you did not complete the aquatic nuisance vegetation monitoring,
aquatic nuisance vegetation control, project staff training, or public outreach and
education measures as required by the license article; and (3) you have documented an
increase in aquatic nuisance vegetation (which has led to the degradation of the lake for
homeowners and recreational users) without implementing management actions to
achieve the objectives of the ANVMP approved by the Order Modifying and Approving
Aquatic Nuisance Vegetation Management Plan (2016 Order). In our letter, we
specifically asked you to: 1) file the missing VMP reports as required by the 2008 Order
within 60 days; and 2) file a plan and schedule to implement the requirements of Article
405 of the project license for Commission approval within 120 days of receipt of the
Commission letter. The Commission’s letter included an attached Schedule A that
outlined the requirements of Article 405 and the 2008 and 2016 Orders. You were
required to develop the plan and schedule in consultation with the U.S. Bureau of
Reclamation (BOR), U.S. Bureau of Land Management (BLM), California Department of
Fish and Game (California DFW), Calaveras County, and Tuolumne County, allowing a
minimum of 30 days for the consulted entities to commend and to make
recommendations before filing the plan with the Commission. You were required to
include documentation of consultation with the specified entities, copies of comments,
and recommendations made in connection with the plan, and a description of how the

requirements of Article 405, during the 2026 growing season; (2) manually removing

the feasibility of GIS-based mapping to identify the species, location, and extent of
coverage of terrestrial noxious weeds and aquatic nuisance vegetation;4 (4) initiating

Boating and Waterways (California DBW),5 the University of California Cooperative
Extension (UCCE),6 and a qualified consultant to support the development of survey
methodology, species identification, and vegetation management efforts, allowing
consulting parties a minimum of 30 days to review and comment on all survey results and
reports; (5) filing the 2026 terrestrial noxious weed survey and aquatic nuisance
vegetation survey reports with the Commission by December 31, 2026, including survey

implementing annual terrestrial noxious weed and aquatic nuisance vegetation
monitoring and control measures consistent with the requirements of license Article 405,
beginning in 2026. You also indicated you would provide further details regarding the

On June 9, 2026, Commission staff received a letter which asserted that your April

Process Plan delays implementation of aquatic nuisance vegetation control measures until

Commenters request that FERC require immediate 2026 season aquatic vegetation

remaining requirements of Article 405, pursuant to the 2008 and 2016 Orders.18 Based

outreach. You address terrestrial noxious weed and aquatic nuisance vegetation

and education, and staff training), the VMP and ANVMP are separate resource plans, and

For these reasons, Commission staff requires that you file a plan and schedule to
satisfy the requirements of license Article 405, pursuant to the 2008 and 2016 orders, as
outlined in the attached Schedule A in consultation with the required resource agencies.
You would then need to file any proposed amendments with the Commission for review
and approval after providing sufficient time for stakeholder consultation. Commission

Ordered plans (Action Items and Next Steps, below).
Conclusions
Commission staff finds that you have timely filed a plan and schedule to file an
updated ANVMP, to comply with the aquatic nuisance vegetation monitoring and control
requirements of license Article 405, pursuant to the 2008 and 2016 Orders, as outlined
the February 3, 2026 Commission letter. However, upon review of the available
information, Commission staff finds that you remain in violation of Article 405 of the
project license on the basis that: (1) you did not complete the terrestrial noxious weed
monitoring and terrestrial noxious weed control requirements, beginning in 2010,
pursuant to the 2008 Order; (2) you failed to implement the approved measure for the
control of sudden oak death within the project area, as specified by the 2008 Order; (3)
you did not provide a plan and schedule to implement the approved aquatic nuisance
vegetation control methods within the project area, as required by the February 3, 2026
Commission letter; (4) you did not include documentation of your public outreach efforts,
as required by the February 3, 2026 Commission letter; and (5) you did not include the
details of any approval process that allows landowners to implement specific methods
that would control or eradicate aquatic nuisance vegetation pursuant to the February 3,
2026 Commission letter. You will remain in violation of Article 405 until you complete
the requirements as outlined above. These ongoing violations will be made a part of the
compliance history for the Project and taken into consideration regarding any future
similar events, and to determine future Commission action.
Commission staff acknowledges your efforts to develop a new plan to monitor and
control aquatic nuisance vegetation. However, Commission staff also notes that your
primary responsibility, as the licensee, is to properly implement the terms of the project
license.

Subject: 2026 Dam Safety Inspection Follow-Up, Bigfork Hydroelectric Project
Dear Mr. Shallenberger:
On August 19, 2026, Mr. Kareem Bynoe and Mr. Dennis Hanneman performed an
inspection of the Bigfork Hydroelectric Project, FERC No. 2652. The project features
were inspected and no conditions were found that would require immediate remedial
action to protect the safety of the project.
Bigfork Diversion Dam (FED ID: MT00220) is in Poor condition based on the
National Inventory of Dams (NID) Condition Assessment definitions. Seepage and
evidence of internal erosion have been observed at the right embankment. Based on our
review, PacifiCorp has implemented appropriate interim risk reduction measures
(IRRMs) while remediation planning is under way. We did not observe any conditions
during the inspection that would change this Condition Assessment rating nor warrant the
implementation of additional IRRMs.
The items listed below were discussed with Mr. Zachary Kocaj during the
inspection and will require follow-up actions by PacifiCorp:
1. Decaying vegetation, consisting of a root mass, was observed at the outlet of the
right embankment toe drain. Upon closer inspection, Operations staff were able to
manually remove an approximately 4-foot-long by 2-inch-thick root and debris
mass from the toe drain. The root mass in the toe drain is not an immediate dam
safety concern but does directly influence the toe drain flow measurements and
could lead to inaccurate drain flow readings. In addition, prolonged unaddressed
obstructions to the toe drain could lead to a complete blockage of the drain,
reducing its effectiveness at conveying seepage. PacifiCorp should review the

2
monitoring procedures for the right embankment toe drain and include clearing
debris from the toe drain outlet as a part of the monitoring program before drain
flow readings are recorded.
2. Evidence of woody vegetation growing on the downstream slope of the right
embankment was observed and has the potential to create additional seepage
pathways as it matures. In addition, grassy vegetation should be maintained to a
reasonable height on a periodic basis to allow for continuous unobstructed visual
observation of the embankments. On the day of the inspection, the grassy
vegetation was long and matted in sections at the right embankment, directly
impacting visual observations. PacifiCorp should review its current vegetation
management procedures to ensure woody vegetation and long grass are
discouraged from being established.
3. As documented in previous dam safety inspections, concrete deterioration was
observed at several Bigfork project structures, e.g., the decommissioned fish
ladder, diversion dam, upper concrete flume, forebay, and ice chute. PacifiCorp
should continue to prioritize repairs at these project structures to facilitate
continued safe access for operations staff and minimize the potential for a
prolonged outage.
4. Based on discussion with Mr. Kocaj, it is our understanding PacifiCorp is in the
early planning stages to make concrete repairs to an isolated location of the upper
concrete box flume. Based on our observations and recent incidents, we concur
with PacifiCorp prioritizing repairs to this area. We also encourage PacifiCorp to
make additional repairs to areas along the north side of the upper concrete box
flume that are significantly deteriorated and where vegetation was observed to be
established in a deteriorated pocket.
5. We observed a void near the interface of the buried HDPE flowline and forebay.
At the time of the inspection, there was no standing water or evidence of soft
material around the edges or in the interior of the void when probed. PacifiCorp
should further investigate this area to determine the extent of the void and provide
a repair plan to fix this area.
6. As documented in previous inspections, woody vegetation (trees) was observed to
be growing along the restored slope adjacent to the lower concrete flume. The
woody vegetation growing in the restored slope area should be controlled or
removed.
Please note that if we identify any additional items requiring follow-up action
during preparation of our Dam Safety Inspection Report, we will contact you by phone
and/or email and subsequently issue another letter.

3
Within 60 days of the date of this letter, please respond to or submit a plan and
schedule to address the comments above. File your submittal using the Commission’s
eFiling system at https://www.ferc.gov/ferc-online/overview. When eFiling, select
Hydro: Dam Safety and Portland Regional Office from the eFiling menu. The cover page
of the filing must indicate that the material was eFiled. For assistance with eFiling,
contact FERC Online Support at FERCOnlineSupport@ferc.gov, (866) 208-3676 (toll
free), or (202) 502-8659 (TTY).
Thank you for your continued cooperation and interest in dam safety. If you have
any questions, please contact Mr. Kareem Bynoe of this office at (503) 552-2719.
Sincerely,
Eric Kennedy, P.E.
Regional Engineer

2022. We encourage you to read this letter in its entirety, as well as the regulations

General Requirements
Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) Title 18, Part 12, Subpart D establishes the
Commission’s Independent Consultant (IC) Inspection Program, also referred to as the
Part 12D Program, and prescribes the scope of inspections, reports, qualifications of
Independent Consultant Team (IC Team) personnel, and related procedures.1 The Part
12D Program is implemented by the Commission’s Office of Energy Projects, Division
of Dam Safety and Inspections (D2SI). Chapter 16 of the Commission’s Engineering
Guidelines for the Evaluation of Hydropower Projects (Engineering Guidelines) provides
additional information related to the Part 12D Program.2

for this inspection:

Guidelines provides an outline for the PIR.

Engineering Guidelines. If the PI-PIPR is acceptable or generally acceptable, the Part
12D Inspection may proceed as scheduled, though we may request follow-up action(s) to
be completed prior to the first activity. If the PI-PIPR is unacceptable, the Part 12D
Inspection will be postponed, and that postponement will not constitute good cause for an
extension to submit the PIR. If the Regional Engineer does not issue a letter within two
weeks after the PI-PIPR is submitted, the PI-PIPR will be deemed acceptable by default.
Field Inspection
The scope of any Part 12D Inspection includes “a physical field inspection of
accessible project works, including galleries, adits, vaults, conduits, earthen and concrete-
lined spillway chutes, the exterior of water conveyances, and other non-submerged
project features that may require specialized access to facilitate inspection.” Section 16-
5.3.1 of the Engineering Guidelines contains additional details regarding inspection of the
reservoir rim and spillway chutes; observation of gate operations; and the review of
special inspection reports.
You must provide a schedule for the field inspection to the Regional Office in
advance of the inspection. If the IC Team intends to split into smaller groups to inspect
multiple project features simultaneously, you must inform us well in advance. Typically,
Regional Office staff will accompany the IC Team during the field inspection, and we
will need to ensure that we send sufficient personnel to observe the project features with
the IC Team. Any special access procedures and safety equipment should be identified
ahead of time so that everyone attending the field inspection can prepare accordingly.
Potential Failure Modes Analysis and Risk Analysis Not Required
The scope of a PI does not include a Potential Failure Modes Analysis (PFMA) or
Level 2 Risk Analysis (L2RA). The IC Team is still responsible for reviewing the most
recent PFMA so they understand each identified PFM prior to the inspection and evaluate
“whether any inspection observations or other conditions indicate that an unidentified
potential failure mode is active, developing, or is of sufficient concern to warrant
development through a supplemental potential failure mode analysis.”8
Periodic Inspection Report
By the due date shown above, you are to submit the IC Team’s PIR to this office.
Section 16-5 of the Engineering Guidelines contains additional information about the
documentation required in each section of the PIR. Please note the following specific
requirements that are important for you and the IC Team to fully understand:
8 18 CFR § 12.36(b)(3)

6
• Incorporation by Reference. The regulations implemented by Order 122 (January
28, 1981) permitted the incorporation by specific reference to a previous Part 12D
Report if the conditions, assumptions, and available information had not changed.
This is not permitted under the regulations that were implemented by Order
880 and which went into effect on April 11, 2022. The IC Team must document
their own interpretation and evaluation in each section of the PIR, where required.
• Evaluation of Performance. The evaluation of the performance of project works
must be an independent interpretation based on the IC Team’s visual observations
and review of instrumentation data and surveillance reports. The IC Team may not
rely entirely on previous interpretations or state that a particular condition or
instrumentation data does not indicate a potential issue simply because it is not
changing over time. The evaluation must clearly address the identified PFMs as
well as whether any previously unidentified PFMs may be active or developing.
• Recommendations. For each corrective measure the IC Team provides in the PIR,
they are also required to provide their recommendation of a reasonable time for
the Licensee to carry out the corrective measure.
Corrective Measures – IC Team Recommendations and Licensee Plan and Schedule
Within 60 days of submitting the Part 12D Report, you must submit your plan and
schedule for addressing any recommendations provided by the IC Team.9 Your plan may
include any proposal, including taking no action, that you consider a preferred alternative
to any corrective measures recommended by the IC Team, and you may not concur with
the IC Team’s recommended time to complete each corrective measure. However, it is
your responsibility to provide complete justification in support of your preferred
alternative, and the Regional Engineer may require modifications to your proposed plan
and schedule.10 You must submit an annual report documenting the status of the
corrective measures until all have been completed.11
If during the course of their inspection, the IC Team discovers any condition for
which emergency corrective measures are advisable, the IC Team must notify you
immediately and you must notify the Regional Engineer pursuant to 18 CFR § 12.10(a).12
Closing
The Commission’s dam safety program is a cooperative process that includes the
Licensee, the IC Team, and the FERC. The most important of the three elements is the

12 18 CFR § 12.41(b)

7
Licensee, as you operate the project, see the project on a regular basis, and are
responsible for the performance monitoring program used to determine if any potential
failure modes are developing. It is your responsibility as the Licensee to submit the Part
12D Report to the FERC and ensure that the Part 12D Report meets the requirements of
the Commission’s Regulations and the Engineering Guidelines before it is submitted. The
Part 12D Report is a FERC requirement but is also a valuable resource for you as the dam
owner.
Except for the Part 12D Inspection Plan, which is discussed above, file the
